questions.text: The Parthenon's peristasis (outer colonnade) arrangement features how many columns on the short ends and long sides?

options.text: 6 columns on short ends and 12 on long sides (6×12 arrangement)
6 columns on short ends and 13 on long sides (6×13 arrangement)
8 columns on short ends and 17 on long sides (8×17 arrangement)
10 columns on short ends and 20 on long sides (10×20 arrangement)

rationale.a: The 6×12 arrangement is not documented for the Parthenon.
rationale.b: The 6×13 arrangement is found on other Doric temples like the Temple of Hephaestus, which is smaller than the Parthenon.
rationale.d: The 10×20 arrangement is not a documented classical Greek order.
rationale.correct: Its plan is a rectangular naos with an outer colonnade (peristasis) of 8 columns on the short ends and 17 columns on the long sides. This 8 × 17 arrangement is standard.'

questions.text: Classical Greek architecture spans approximately which time period?

options.text: c. 1200–800 BCE (Bronze Age), a period characterized by early architectural developments
c. 900–146 BCE (Archaic through Hellenistic periods)
c. 500–146 BCE (Classical period only), focusing on the height of Greek architectural innovation
c. 800–300 BCE (Iron Age), which saw the transition from simple to more complex structures

rationale.a: 1200–800 BCE is too early and represents the Bronze Age, before the development of the Greek architectural tradition.
rationale.c: While Classical period is covered, the architectural tradition spanned from the Archaic period (900 BCE onward).
rationale.d: While 800 BCE is close, the date of 900 BCE is more accurate for the beginning of Greek architectural development.
rationale.correct: Greek architecture (c. 900–146 BCE) abandoned the massive walls and hypostyle halls of earlier civilizations.'
rationale.takeaway: 900–146 BCE) abandoned the massive walls and hypostyle halls of earlier civilizations.'.

questions.text: The Parthenon, built on the Acropolis at Athens between 447–432 BCE, was designed by which two architects?

options.text: Libon and Kallikrates
Iktinos and Kallikrates
Phidias and Polyclitus
Hippodamus and Polyclitus

rationale.a: Libon designed the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, not the Parthenon.
rationale.c: Phidias oversaw the sculpture program, not the architectural design; Polyclitus designed the Tholos at Epidaurus.
rationale.d: Hippodamus designed the city of Miletus; Polyclitus designed the Tholos at Epidaurus.
rationale.correct: The Parthenon (Temple of Athena Parthenos): Built on the Acropolis at Athens between 447–432 BCE under the direction of the general Pericles, designed by Iktinos and Kallikrates, with sculpture overseen by Phidias.'
rationale.takeaway: The article states: 'The Parthenon (Temple of Athena Parthenos): Built on the Acropolis at Athens between 447–432 BCE under the direction of the general Pericles, designed by Iktinos and Kallikrates, with sculpture overseen by Phidias.'.

questions.text: A Greek column capital features two spiraling scrolls (volutes) and a base, and the entablature above includes a continuous frieze often sculpted with narrative scenes. Which order does this describe?

options.text: Doric order
Ionic order
Corinthian order
Tuscan order

rationale.a: The Doric order has a simple capital without volutes and a triglyph-metope entablature, not a continuous frieze.
rationale.c: The Corinthian order features acanthus leaves and other scrollwork, not just volutes.
rationale.d: The Tuscan order is a Roman order, not a Greek order.
rationale.correct: The Ionic order: 'An Ionic column is 8–10 times its diameter in height, with a base (unlike Doric) and a capital featuring two spiraling scrolls (volutes). The entablature is simpler: a continuous frieze (often sculpted) runs above the columns.'
rationale.takeaway: The entablature is simpler: a continuous frieze (often sculpted) runs above the columns.'.

questions.text: The Doric order is characterized by which proportional relationship between column height and diameter?

options.text: Roughly 8–10 times its diameter
Roughly 10+ times its diameter
Roughly 4–6 times its diameter
Roughly 2–3 times its diameter

rationale.a: This is the proportion of the Ionic order (8–10 times).
rationale.b: This is the proportion of the Corinthian order (10+ times).
rationale.d: This is not a documented classical Greek column proportion.
rationale.correct: Doric Order: The earliest and most austere. A Doric column is squat and sturdy, roughly 4–6 times its diameter in height.'
rationale.takeaway: A Doric column is squat and sturdy, roughly 4–6 times its diameter in height.'.

questions.text: A student must distinguish between Doric and Ionic orders. Which set of characteristics correctly differentiates them?

options.text: Doric columns are slender (8–10 diameters), lack a base, and feature acanthus-leaf capitals; Ionic columns are stocky (4–6 diameters) with simple capitals, which is a common error in identification.

Doric columns are squat and sturdy (4–6 diameters), with a simple capital and triglyph-metope entablature; Ionic columns are more slender (8–10 diameters), with a base and volute capital, and have a continuous frieze entablature
Both orders are identical, with differences only in regional naming conventions, which is a misconception.
Doric appears only in mainland Greece; Ionic appears only in Asia Minor (Turkey), which oversimplifies their historical distribution.

rationale.a: This reverses the proportions and capital features; Doric is squat with simple capitals, not slender with acanthus leaves.
rationale.c: The orders have distinct proportions, capital forms, and entablature designs.
rationale.d: While Ionic appeared first in Asia Minor, both orders were used across Greek regions by the Classical period.
rationale.correct: This option correctly identifies the proportional, capital, and entablature distinctions documented in the article.
rationale.takeaway: This option correctly identifies the proportional, capital, and entablature distinctions documented in the article.

questions.text: A circular Greek temple structure with an internal colonnade and a circular plan rather than rectangular is called:

options.text: Stoa
Tholos
Cella
Peristyle

rationale.a: A stoa is a portico or covered walkway with columns, not a circular temple.
rationale.c: Cella (or naos) is the inner chamber of a temple, not a circular building type.
rationale.d: Peristyle refers to a colonnade surrounding a building, not a specific circular building type.
rationale.correct: The Treasury of Atreus at Mycenae (c. 1350 BCE, pre-Classical but influential) featured a corbelled dome—a "tholos" or circular structure that predates Greek post-and-lintel temples. Later Greek architects revived the tholos form for certain temples and treasuries, such as the Tholos of Polyclitus at Epidaurus (c. 360 BCE).'
rationale.takeaway: Later Greek architects revived the tholos form for certain temples and treasuries, such as the Tholos of Polyclitus at Epidaurus (c. 360 BCE).'.

questions.text: Greek temple construction employed stone drums stacked vertically to form columns. This approach allowed for which architectural advantage?

options.text: Reducing the total weight of the structure through modular construction
Enabling the creation of entasis through controlled reductions in diameter between drums
Allowing easier transport and positioning of individual sections compared to monolithic columns
All of the above

rationale.a: While modularity has benefits, this alone is incomplete.
rationale.b: While entasis is enabled, this alone is incomplete.
rationale.c: While transport is easier, this alone is incomplete.
rationale.correct: Unlike Egyptian stone construction (massive blocks set by weight), Greek builders cut stone to economical sizes and fitted them with dowels and clamps of bronze or lead. The columns were built in drums (cylindrical sections) stacked vertically. Entasis (the slight curve) was achieved by subtle reductions in diameter between drums.' This accomplishes all three advantages.
rationale.takeaway: Entasis (the slight curve) was achieved by subtle reductions in diameter between drums.' This accomplishes all three advantages.

questions.text: A student studies both Greek post-and-lintel temples and Roman arch-vault buildings and concludes they represent the same structural tradition. Which statement best corrects this misconception?

options.text: Greek and Roman architecture are identical; all differences are superficial, with no significant structural variations between them
Greek temples use post-and-lintel systems with limited interior span; Roman buildings use arches and vaults enabling vast interior spaces—these are fundamentally different structural approaches
Greeks invented the arch, which Romans later refined and adapted for their own architectural styles
Roman architecture was an early stage of Greek development, eventually evolving into its own distinct form

rationale.a: The systems are fundamentally different, not superficially different.
rationale.c: Greeks used post-and-lintel; the arch was a Roman innovation in this context.
rationale.d: Roman architecture developed later and independently, not from Greek precedent in structural innovation.
rationale.correct: The article addresses this: 'Confusing Greek (post-and-lintel) with Roman (arch-vault) architecture. Greeks used columns and entablatures; Romans added arches, vaults, and concrete. These are distinct systems. Do not describe Greek buildings with Roman terminology.'
rationale.takeaway: Do not describe Greek buildings with Roman terminology.'.

questions.text: Why did Greek architects employ entasis (the subtle inward curve of columns) in structures like the Parthenon?

options.text: To reduce the weight of the column and allow for taller structures, which was a common goal in ancient Greek architecture
As a cost-saving measure to use less stone material, which was a significant consideration in large-scale constructions
To counteract the optical distortion that makes straight lines appear to sag, creating the illusion of straightness and proper form
To provide better wind resistance and structural stability against earthquakes, which were frequent in the region

rationale.a: Entasis adds material, not reduces it; it was not a weight-saving measure.
rationale.b: The opposite is true; entasis requires more precise stone cutting and thus more labor and expense.
rationale.d: While the curvature might provide some structural benefit, the documented purpose is visual correction.
rationale.correct: Entasis (the slight curve) was achieved by subtle reductions in diameter between drums' and clarifies a common mistake: 'Treating entasis as a defect. Entasis (the curve) is not accidental but calculated. It's a visual correction for the illusion of sagging that straight lines create. Treat it as evidence of sophistication, not weakness.'
rationale.takeaway: Treat it as evidence of sophistication, not weakness.'.

questions.text: Why did Greek architects and sculptors invest such detailed effort in the Parthenon's interior sculptural program, even though most viewers would not have access to the interior to see it?

options.text: The interior decoration served no purpose and was merely a waste of resources, reflecting a lack of practical consideration in the design process
The Parthenon served as a treasury and a sanctuary, making the interior as important as the exterior; the interior decoration served religious and administrative functions
The interior was purely decorative, intended only for the priesthood's personal appreciation, emphasizing exclusivity and spiritual hierarchy
The sculptural program was added after the building's completion and served no original purpose, indicating a later adaptation to changing cultural or religious needs

rationale.a: The interior decoration was integral to the building's function, not wasteful.
rationale.c: While priests accessed the interior, the building's function was not personal appreciation but religious and administrative.
rationale.d: The sculptural program was part of the original design (447–432 BCE), not a later addition.
rationale.correct: The Parthenon housed a chryselephantine (gold and ivory) statue of Athena, 40+ feet tall, now lost. The sculptural program included a continuous frieze around the naos depicting the Panathenaic procession, and pediment sculptures. The Parthenon's interior was as important as its exterior; it was a treasury and a sanctuary, not merely a visual monument.'
rationale.takeaway: The Parthenon's interior was as important as its exterior; it was a treasury and a sanctuary, not merely a visual monument.'.

questions.text: Sculpted femlea figures serving as columns or vertical supports in Greek architecture are called:

options.text: Kouroi, which are typically male statues used in different contexts
Atlantes, which are male figures used as supports, differing from female caryatids
Caryatids
Herms, which are square pillars with a head on top, not used as columns

rationale.a: Kouroi are nude male sculptures in archaic Greek art, not figures serving as columns.
rationale.b: Atlantes are male figures serving as supports (the male equivalent of caryatids); caryatids are female.
rationale.d: Herms are boundary markers or posts topped with a bust of Hermes, not columns.
rationale.correct: The article defines: 'Caryatid (or Caryatids): A sculpted female figure serving as a column or support; seen in the Porch of the Maidens at the Erechtheion.'
rationale.takeaway: The article defines: 'Caryatid (or Caryatids): A sculpted female figure serving as a column or support; seen in the Porch of the Maidens at the Erechtheion.'.
